verses.text: In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth.
verses.displayText: In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth.
verses.context: This is the very first line of the Bible, spoken by the narrator before any person exists to hear it.

verses.text: And God said, Let there be light: and there was light.
verses.displayText: And God said, Let there be light: and there was light.
verses.context: Still in the creation account, the narrator describes God speaking light into existence on the first day.

verses.text: So God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them.
verses.displayText: So God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them.
verses.context: Continuing the creation account, the narrator describes God making the first humans, male and female.

verses.text: Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh.
verses.displayText: Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh.
verses.context: The narrator pauses right after the first woman is created to explain why a man and woman become one family through marriage.

verses.text: I do set my bow in the cloud, and it shall be for a token of a covenant between me and the earth.
verses.displayText: I do set my bow in the cloud, and it shall be for a token of a covenant between me and the earth.
verses.context: After the flood story ends, God speaks to Noah and his family, giving them a sign that he will never flood the whole earth again.

verses.text: And he believed in the Lord; and he counted it to him for righteousness.
verses.displayText: And he believed in the Lord; and he counted it to him for righteousness.
verses.context: The narrator describes Abram's response after God promised him more descendants than he could count, though he had none yet.

verses.text: And, behold, I am with thee, and will keep thee in all places whither thou goest, and will bring thee again into this land; for I will not leave thee, until I have done that which I have spoken to thee of.
verses.displayText: And, behold, I am with thee, and will keep thee in all places whither thou goest, and will bring thee again into this land; for I will not leave thee, until I have done that which I have spoken to thee of.
verses.context: Fleeing his brother's anger, Jacob is alone at night when God speaks to him in a dream, promising to bring him home safely.

verses.text: But as for you, ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good, to bring to pass, as it is this day, to save much people alive.
verses.displayText: But as for you, ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good, to bring to pass, as it is this day, to save much people alive.
verses.context: Years after his brothers sold him into slavery, Joseph, now a powerful official in Egypt, reassures them that he holds no grudge.

verses.text: And God said unto Moses, I AM THAT I AM: and he said, Thus shalt thou say unto the children of Israel, I AM hath sent me unto you.
verses.displayText: And God said unto Moses, I AM THAT I AM: and he said, Thus shalt thou say unto the children of Israel, I AM hath sent me unto you.
verses.context: Moses, tending sheep in the desert, asks a voice from a burning bush what name he should give the people of Israel.

verses.text: The Lord shall fight for you, and ye shall hold your peace.
verses.displayText: The Lord shall fight for you, and ye shall hold your peace.
verses.context: Trapped between the sea and Pharaoh's army, Moses tells the terrified Israelites not to fight but to stay calm.

verses.text: Thou shalt have no other gods before me.
verses.displayText: Thou shalt have no other gods before me.
verses.context: This is the first of the Ten Commandments, given to Moses on Mount Sinai for the people of Israel.

verses.text: Honour thy father and thy mother: that thy days may be long upon the land which the Lord thy God giveth thee.
verses.displayText: Honour thy father and thy mother: that thy days may be long upon the land which the Lord thy God giveth thee.
verses.context: Part of the Ten Commandments Moses received on Mount Sinai, this one concerns how children should treat their parents.

verses.text: Thou shalt not kill.
verses.displayText: Thou shalt not kill.
verses.context: One of the Ten Commandments given to Moses on Mount Sinai, a short, direct rule against killing.

verses.text: And he said, My presence shall go with thee, and I will give thee rest.
verses.displayText: And he said, My presence shall go with thee, and I will give thee rest.
verses.context: After the people had angered God by worshipping an idol, Moses asks for reassurance, and God answers him directly.

verses.text: Thou shalt not avenge, nor bear any grudge against the children of thy people, but thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself: I am the Lord.
verses.displayText: Thou shalt not avenge, nor bear any grudge against the children of thy people, but thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself: I am the Lord.
verses.context: Part of a long list of laws Moses gave Israel, this one tells people how to treat their neighbors instead of holding grudges.

verses.text: The Lord bless thee, and keep thee:
verses.displayText: The Lord bless thee, and keep thee:
verses.context: God gives Moses these exact words for the priests Aaron and his sons to say over the people of Israel.

verses.text: God is not a man, that he should lie; neither the son of man, that he should repent: hath he said, and shall he not do it? or hath he spoken, and shall he not make it good?
verses.displayText: God is not a man, that he should lie; neither the son of man, that he should repent: hath he said, and shall he not do it? or hath he spoken, and shall he not make it good?
verses.context: Hired by a hostile king to curse Israel, the prophet Balaam instead speaks a blessing he says came from God.

verses.text: But if from thence thou shalt seek the Lord thy God, thou shalt find him, if thou seek him with all thy heart and with all thy soul.
verses.displayText: But if from thence thou shalt seek the Lord thy God, thou shalt find him, if thou seek him with all thy heart and with all thy soul.
verses.context: Near the end of his life, Moses reminds the Israelites what will happen if they turn back to God after going astray.

verses.text: I call heaven and earth to record this day against you, that I have set before you life and death, blessing and cursing: therefore choose life, that both thou and thy seed may live:
verses.displayText: I call heaven and earth to record this day against you, that I have set before you life and death, blessing and cursing: therefore choose life, that both thou and thy seed may live:
verses.context: In his final speech before the people cross into the new land without him, Moses lays out a choice between two paths.

verses.text: Have not I commanded thee? Be strong and of a good courage; be not afraid, neither be thou dismayed: for the Lord thy God is with thee whithersoever thou goest.
verses.displayText: Have not I commanded thee? Be strong and of a good courage; be not afraid, neither be thou dismayed: for the Lord thy God is with thee whithersoever thou goest.
verses.context: After Moses's death, God speaks directly to Joshua, his successor, as he prepares to lead Israel into the new land.

verses.text: And if it seem evil unto you to serve the Lord, choose you this day whom ye will serve; whether the gods which your fathers served that were on the other side of the flood, or the gods of the Amorites, in whose land ye dwell: but as for me and my house, we will serve the Lord.
verses.displayText: And if it seem evil unto you to serve the Lord, choose you this day whom ye will serve; whether the gods which your fathers served that were on the other side of the flood, or the gods of the Amorites, in whose land ye dwell: but as for me and my house, we will serve the Lord.
verses.context: Near the end of his life, Joshua gathers the tribes of Israel and challenges them to decide who they will serve.

verses.text: And Ruth said, Intreat me not to leave thee, or to return from following after thee: for whither thou goest, I will go; and where thou lodgest, I will lodge: thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God:
verses.displayText: And Ruth said, Intreat me not to leave thee, or to return from following after thee: for whither thou goest, I will go; and where thou lodgest, I will lodge: thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God:
verses.context: A widow from Moab, Ruth refuses to leave her mother-in-law Naomi and go back to her own people.

verses.text: And the Lord came, and stood, and called as at other times, Samuel, Samuel. Then Samuel answered, Speak; for thy servant heareth.
verses.displayText: And the Lord came, and stood, and called as at other times, Samuel, Samuel. Then Samuel answered, Speak; for thy servant heareth.
verses.context: A boy serving in the temple, Samuel hears a voice calling his name at night and, guided by the old priest Eli, answers it.

verses.text: But the Lord said unto Samuel, Look not on his countenance, or on the height of his stature; because I have refused him: for the Lord seeth not as man seeth; for man looketh on the outward appearance, but the Lord looketh on the heart.
verses.displayText: But the Lord said unto Samuel, Look not on his countenance, or on the height of his stature; because I have refused him: for the Lord seeth not as man seeth; for man looketh on the outward appearance, but the Lord looketh on the heart.
verses.context: Sent to anoint Israel's next king, the prophet Samuel is about to pick Jesse's oldest son by his looks when God stops him.

verses.text: And David was greatly distressed; for the people spake of stoning him, because the soul of all the people was grieved, every man for his sons and for his daughters: but David encouraged himself in the Lord his God.
verses.displayText: And David was greatly distressed; for the people spake of stoning him, because the soul of all the people was grieved, every man for his sons and for his daughters: but David encouraged himself in the Lord his God.
verses.context: Dismissed by the Philistines before any battle, David arrives home to find his camp burned and family taken, his men talking of stoning him.

verses.text: And Elijah came unto all the people, and said, How long halt ye between two opinions? if the Lord be God, follow him: but if Baal, then follow him. And the people answered him not a word.
verses.displayText: And Elijah came unto all the people, and said, How long halt ye between two opinions? if the Lord be God, follow him: but if Baal, then follow him. And the people answered him not a word.
verses.context: On Mount Carmel, the prophet Elijah confronts a crowd of Israelites who have been worshipping both God and the god Baal.

verses.text: And after the earthquake a fire; but the Lord was not in the fire: and after the fire a still small voice.
verses.displayText: And after the earthquake a fire; but the Lord was not in the fire: and after the fire a still small voice.
verses.context: Hiding in a cave after fleeing a death threat, Elijah waits through wind, an earthquake, and fire for God to speak.

verses.text: And he answered, Fear not: for they that be with us are more than they that be with them.
verses.displayText: And he answered, Fear not: for they that be with us are more than they that be with them.
verses.context: Surrounded by an enemy army, Elisha's frightened servant is told not to be afraid, since more is on their side than he can see.

verses.text: And Jabez called on the God of Israel, saying, Oh that thou wouldest bless me indeed, and enlarge my coast, and that thine hand might be with me, and that thou wouldest keep me from evil, that it may not grieve me! And God granted him that which he requested.
verses.displayText: And Jabez called on the God of Israel, saying, Oh that thou wouldest bless me indeed, and enlarge my coast, and that thine hand might be with me, and that thou wouldest keep me from evil, that it may not grieve me! And God granted him that which he requested.
verses.context: In a long list of family names, the narrator pauses to record a prayer from a man named Jabez, asking God to bless and protect him.

verses.text: Seek the Lord and his strength, seek his face continually.
verses.displayText: Seek the Lord and his strength, seek his face continually.
verses.context: In a song David wrote for the priests to sing when Israel's sacred ark arrived in Jerusalem, worshippers are urged to seek God.

verses.text: If my people, which are called by my name, shall humble themselves, and pray, and seek my face, and turn from their wicked ways; then will I hear from heaven, and will forgive their sin, and will heal their land.
verses.displayText: If my people, which are called by my name, shall humble themselves, and pray, and seek my face, and turn from their wicked ways; then will I hear from heaven, and will forgive their sin, and will heal their land.
verses.context: After Solomon finishes building the temple, God appears to him at night with a promise about what happens when the nation turns back after wrong.

verses.text: And he said, Hearken ye, all Judah, and ye inhabitants of Jerusalem, and thou king Jehoshaphat, Thus saith the Lord unto you, Be not afraid nor dismayed by reason of this great multitude; for the battle is not yours, but God’s.
verses.displayText: And he said, Hearken ye, all Judah, and ye inhabitants of Jerusalem, and thou king Jehoshaphat, Thus saith the Lord unto you, Be not afraid nor dismayed by reason of this great multitude; for the battle is not yours, but God’s.
verses.context: Facing a massive invading army, King Jehoshaphat and the people of Judah hear a prophet named Jahaziel tell them not to be afraid.

verses.text: Then he said unto them, Go your way, eat the fat, and drink the sweet, and send portions unto them for whom nothing is prepared: for this day is holy unto our Lord: neither be ye sorry; for the joy of the Lord is your strength.
verses.displayText: Then he said unto them, Go your way, eat the fat, and drink the sweet, and send portions unto them for whom nothing is prepared: for this day is holy unto our Lord: neither be ye sorry; for the joy of the Lord is your strength.
verses.context: After exiles returning to Jerusalem hear the law read aloud and weep, the leader Nehemiah tells them to celebrate instead.

verses.text: For if thou altogether holdest thy peace at this time, then shall there enlargement and deliverance arise to the Jews from another place; but thou and thy father’s house shall be destroyed: and who knoweth whether thou art come to the kingdom for such a time as this?
verses.displayText: For if thou altogether holdest thy peace at this time, then shall there enlargement and deliverance arise to the Jews from another place; but thou and thy father’s house shall be destroyed: and who knoweth whether thou art come to the kingdom for such a time as this?
verses.context: Esther's cousin Mordecai sends her this message, urging her to risk approaching the king to save her people from destruction.

verses.text: And said, Naked came I out of my mother’s womb, and naked shall I return thither: the Lord gave, and the Lord hath taken away; blessed be the name of the Lord.
verses.displayText: And said, Naked came I out of my mother’s womb, and naked shall I return thither: the Lord gave, and the Lord hath taken away; blessed be the name of the Lord.
verses.context: After losing his children and property in a single day, Job tears his clothes, falls to the ground, and speaks these words.

verses.text: But he said unto her, Thou speakest as one of the foolish women speaketh. What? shall we receive good at the hand of God, and shall we not receive evil? In all this did not Job sin with his lips.
verses.displayText: But he said unto her, Thou speakest as one of the foolish women speaketh. What? shall we receive good at the hand of God, and shall we not receive evil? In all this did not Job sin with his lips.
verses.context: After Job is struck with painful sores, his wife tells him to curse God and die, and this is his reply to her.

verses.text: Though he slay me, yet will I trust in him: but I will maintain mine own ways before him.
verses.displayText: Though he slay me, yet will I trust in him: but I will maintain mine own ways before him.
verses.context: In the middle of arguing with friends who insist his suffering must be punishment, Job insists he will keep trusting God anyway.

verses.text: Man that is born of a woman is of few days, and full of trouble.
verses.displayText: Man that is born of a woman is of few days, and full of trouble.
verses.context: In a long speech about the shortness and hardship of life, Job describes the human condition in general terms.

verses.text: For I know that my redeemer liveth, and that he shall stand at the latter day upon the earth:
verses.displayText: For I know that my redeemer liveth, and that he shall stand at the latter day upon the earth:
verses.context: Despite his friends' accusations and his own suffering, Job insists to them that he still has someone who will defend him in the end.

verses.text: But he knoweth the way that I take: when he hath tried me, I shall come forth as gold.
verses.displayText: But he knoweth the way that I take: when he hath tried me, I shall come forth as gold.
verses.context: Still defending himself to his friends, Job says that even though he cannot find God, God knows exactly what Job is going through.

verses.text: Where wast thou when I laid the foundations of the earth? declare, if thou hast understanding.
verses.displayText: Where wast thou when I laid the foundations of the earth? declare, if thou hast understanding.
verses.context: After Job's long complaint and his friends' failed arguments, God finally speaks to Job out of a storm, questioning him directly.

verses.text: I have heard of thee by the hearing of the ear: but now mine eye seeth thee.
verses.displayText: I have heard of thee by the hearing of the ear: but now mine eye seeth thee.
verses.context: Near the end of the book, after God has questioned him at length, Job replies, describing how his understanding of God has changed.

verses.text: Blessed is the man that walketh not in the counsel of the ungodly, nor standeth in the way of sinners, nor sitteth in the seat of the scornful.
verses.displayText: Blessed is the man that walketh not in the counsel of the ungodly, nor standeth in the way of sinners, nor sitteth in the seat of the scornful.
verses.context: This opens the book of Psalms, describing the kind of person who avoids bad influences and finds happiness elsewhere.

verses.text: And he shall be like a tree planted by the rivers of water, that bringeth forth his fruit in his season; his leaf also shall not wither; and whatsoever he doeth shall prosper.
verses.displayText: And he shall be like a tree planted by the rivers of water, that bringeth forth his fruit in his season; his leaf also shall not wither; and whatsoever he doeth shall prosper.
verses.context: Still in the opening psalm, the writer compares a person who follows good guidance to a tree planted by a river.

verses.text: I will both lay me down in peace, and sleep: for thou, Lord, only makest me dwell in safety.
verses.displayText: I will both lay me down in peace, and sleep: for thou, Lord, only makest me dwell in safety.
verses.context: David wrote this short evening psalm, a simple statement of trust before going to sleep.

verses.text: What is man, that thou art mindful of him? and the son of man, that thou visitest him?
verses.displayText: What is man, that thou art mindful of him? and the son of man, that thou visitest him?
verses.context: Looking up at the night sky, David wonders aloud in this psalm why God would bother paying attention to human beings at all.

verses.text: And they that know thy name will put their trust in thee: for thou, Lord, hast not forsaken them that seek thee.
verses.displayText: And they that know thy name will put their trust in thee: for thou, Lord, hast not forsaken them that seek thee.
verses.context: In a psalm of praise, David reassures the reader that people who truly know God will trust him.

verses.text: Why standest thou afar off, O Lord? why hidest thou thyself in times of trouble?
verses.displayText: Why standest thou afar off, O Lord? why hidest thou thyself in times of trouble?
verses.context: This psalm opens with the writer asking God directly why he feels distant during hard times.

verses.text: Thou wilt shew me the path of life: in thy presence is fulness of joy; at thy right hand there are pleasures for evermore.
verses.displayText: Thou wilt shew me the path of life: in thy presence is fulness of joy; at thy right hand there are pleasures for evermore.
verses.context: In a psalm about trusting God even in death, David ends by describing lasting joy in God's presence.

verses.text: The Lord is my rock, and my fortress, and my deliverer; my God, my strength, in whom I will trust; my buckler, and the horn of my salvation, and my high tower.
verses.displayText: The Lord is my rock, and my fortress, and my deliverer; my God, my strength, in whom I will trust; my buckler, and the horn of my salvation, and my high tower.
verses.context: David wrote this psalm after God rescued him from his enemies, including King Saul, who had hunted him for years.

verses.text: To the chief Musician, A Psalm of David. The heavens declare the glory of God; and the firmament sheweth his handywork.
verses.displayText: The heavens declare the glory of God; and the firmament sheweth his handywork.
verses.context: Looking up at the sky, David describes in this psalm how creation itself seems to announce God's greatness without saying a word.

verses.text: Let the words of my mouth, and the meditation of my heart, be acceptable in thy sight, O Lord, my strength, and my redeemer.
verses.displayText: Let the words of my mouth, and the meditation of my heart, be acceptable in thy sight, O Lord, my strength, and my redeemer.
verses.context: At the close of the same psalm about creation, David turns his praise into a personal prayer about his own words and thoughts.

verses.text: To the chief Musician upon Aijeleth Shahar, A Psalm of David. My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me? why art thou so far from helping me, and from the words of my roaring?
verses.displayText: My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me? why art thou so far from helping me, and from the words of my roaring?
verses.context: David wrote this cry of anguish; centuries later, the Gospels record Jesus quoting these same opening words while dying on the cross.

verses.text: A Psalm of David. The Lord is my shepherd; I shall not want.
verses.displayText: The Lord is my shepherd; I shall not want.
verses.context: David, who had worked as a shepherd before becoming king, opens this well-known psalm by picturing God in that same role.

verses.text: He maketh me to lie down in green pastures: he leadeth me beside the still waters.
verses.displayText: He maketh me to lie down in green pastures: he leadeth me beside the still waters.
verses.context: Continuing the shepherd imagery of the same psalm, David describes the rest and care that image brings to mind.

verses.text: He restoreth my soul: he leadeth me in the paths of righteousness for his name’s sake.
verses.displayText: He restoreth my soul: he leadeth me in the paths of righteousness for his name’s sake.
verses.context: Still using the shepherd image, David describes being guided along the right way.

verses.text: Yea, though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil: for thou art with me; thy rod and thy staff they comfort me.
verses.displayText: Yea, though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil: for thou art with me; thy rod and thy staff they comfort me.
verses.context: The shepherd image turns darker here, as David pictures walking through a valley of deep shadow without fear.

verses.text: Thou preparest a table before me in the presence of mine enemies: thou anointest my head with oil; my cup runneth over.
verses.displayText: Thou preparest a table before me in the presence of mine enemies: thou anointest my head with oil; my cup runneth over.
verses.context: Shifting from shepherd to host, David pictures God preparing a feast for him even while enemies look on.

verses.text: Surely goodness and mercy shall follow me all the days of my life: and I will dwell in the house of the Lord for ever.
verses.displayText: Surely goodness and mercy shall follow me all the days of my life: and I will dwell in the house of the Lord for ever.
verses.context: This closes the psalm, with David expecting kindness to follow him for the rest of his life and beyond.

verses.text: Shew me thy ways, O Lord; teach me thy paths.
verses.displayText: Shew me thy ways, O Lord; teach me thy paths.
verses.context: Trusting God rather than his own judgment, David opens this psalm by asking to be shown which way to go.

verses.text: A Psalm of David. The Lord is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear? the Lord is the strength of my life; of whom shall I be afraid?
verses.displayText: The Lord is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear? the Lord is the strength of my life; of whom shall I be afraid?
verses.context: Facing enemies who wanted him dead, David opens this psalm by declaring where his confidence actually comes from.

verses.text: Wait on the Lord: be of good courage, and he shall strengthen thine heart: wait, I say, on the Lord.
verses.displayText: Wait on the Lord: be of good courage, and he shall strengthen thine heart: wait, I say, on the Lord.
verses.context: David closes this psalm about facing hostile enemies by telling his own heart to keep waiting and stay brave.

verses.text: The Lord is my strength and my shield; my heart trusted in him, and I am helped: therefore my heart greatly rejoiceth; and with my song will I praise him.
verses.displayText: The Lord is my strength and my shield; my heart trusted in him, and I am helped: therefore my heart greatly rejoiceth; and with my song will I praise him.
verses.context: In a psalm asking God not to stay silent, David shifts partway through to thanking God for already helping him.

verses.text: The Lord will give strength unto his people; the Lord will bless his people with peace.
verses.displayText: The Lord will give strength unto his people; the Lord will bless his people with peace.
verses.context: This closes a psalm describing a violent storm as the voice of God, ending with a wish for peace over his people.

verses.text: For his anger endureth but a moment; in his favour is life: weeping may endure for a night, but joy cometh in the morning.
verses.displayText: For his anger endureth but a moment; in his favour is life: weeping may endure for a night, but joy cometh in the morning.
verses.context: Written for the dedication of his house, David's psalm turns from sorrow to joy within a single verse.

verses.text: I will instruct thee and teach thee in the way which thou shalt go: I will guide thee with mine eye.
verses.displayText: I will instruct thee and teach thee in the way which thou shalt go: I will guide thee with mine eye.
verses.context: After describing being forgiven, David reports God speaking directly to him, promising to guide and teach him.

verses.text: O taste and see that the Lord is good: blessed is the man that trusteth in him.
verses.displayText: O taste and see that the Lord is good: blessed is the man that trusteth in him.
verses.context: Written after David pretended to be insane to escape a hostile king, this psalm invites the reader to test God's goodness personally.

verses.text: The righteous cry, and the Lord heareth, and delivereth them out of all their troubles.
verses.displayText: The righteous cry, and the Lord heareth, and delivereth them out of all their troubles.
verses.context: The same psalm continues by describing God listening whenever people in trouble cry out for help.

verses.text: The Lord is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart; and saveth such as be of a contrite spirit.
verses.displayText: The Lord is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart; and saveth such as be of a contrite spirit.
verses.context: Right after that, the same psalm adds that God stays close to anyone who is brokenhearted or crushed in spirit.

verses.text: Delight thyself also in the Lord; and he shall give thee the desires of thine heart.
verses.displayText: Delight thyself also in the Lord; and he shall give thee the desires of thine heart.
verses.context: Advising against envy toward people who do wrong, David offers this alternative instead: finding joy in God himself.

verses.text: Commit thy way unto the Lord; trust also in him; and he shall bring it to pass.
verses.displayText: Commit thy way unto the Lord; trust also in him; and he shall bring it to pass.
verses.context: David goes on immediately to say that handing his plans over to God is what makes them succeed.

verses.text: The steps of a good man are ordered by the Lord: and he delighteth in his way.
verses.displayText: The steps of a good man are ordered by the Lord: and he delighteth in his way.
verses.context: By the end of this wisdom psalm, David describes a good life as something actively directed and steadied by God.

verses.text: Why art thou cast down, O my soul? and why art thou disquieted within me? hope thou in God: for I shall yet praise him, who is the health of my countenance, and my God.
verses.displayText: Why art thou cast down, O my soul? and why art thou disquieted within me? hope thou in God: for I shall yet praise him, who is the health of my countenance, and my God.
verses.context: Talking to his own discouraged heart, the psalm's writer repeats this line as a refrain to talk himself back into hope.

verses.text: To the chief Musician for the sons of Korah, A Song upon Alamoth. God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble.
verses.displayText: God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble.
verses.context: Written by the sons of Korah, a family of temple singers, this psalm opens by naming God as a safe place during disaster.

verses.text: Be still, and know that I am God: I will be exalted among the heathen, I will be exalted in the earth.
verses.displayText: Be still, and know that I am God: I will be exalted among the heathen, I will be exalted in the earth.
verses.context: Near the close of this psalm about disaster and refuge, God himself is quoted telling the nations to stop and take notice.

verses.text: Create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me.
verses.displayText: Create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me.
verses.context: Written after the prophet Nathan confronted him over his affair with Bathsheba, David asks God for a fresh start.

verses.text: Cast thy burden upon the Lord, and he shall sustain thee: he shall never suffer the righteous to be moved.
verses.displayText: Cast thy burden upon the Lord, and he shall sustain thee: he shall never suffer the righteous to be moved.
verses.context: Betrayed by a close friend, David tells himself in this psalm to hand his burden over to God and trust God to hold him up.

verses.text: What time I am afraid, I will trust in thee.
verses.displayText: What time I am afraid, I will trust in thee.
verses.context: Written after the Philistines had captured him in the city of Gath, David admits his fear and where he takes it.

verses.text: Thou tellest my wanderings: put thou my tears into thy bottle: are they not in thy book?
verses.displayText: Thou tellest my wanderings: put thou my tears into thy bottle: are they not in thy book?
verses.context: This same psalm, written while David was a captive, goes on to describe God keeping track of every tear he sheds.

verses.text: From the end of the earth will I cry unto thee, when my heart is overwhelmed: lead me to the rock that is higher than I.
verses.displayText: From the end of the earth will I cry unto thee, when my heart is overwhelmed: lead me to the rock that is higher than I.
verses.context: Praying from somewhere far from home, David asks to be led to a place of safety higher than himself.

verses.text: Verily I have cleansed my heart in vain, and washed my hands in innocency.
verses.displayText: Verily I have cleansed my heart in vain, and washed my hands in innocency.
verses.context: Written by Asaph, a temple musician, this verse voices his doubt after watching wicked people prosper while he suffers.

verses.text: My flesh and my heart faileth: but God is the strength of my heart, and my portion for ever.
verses.displayText: My flesh and my heart faileth: but God is the strength of my heart, and my portion for ever.
verses.context: By the end of this psalm, Asaph's body may be failing, but he describes God as his strength regardless.

verses.text: Hath God forgotten to be gracious? hath he in anger shut up his tender mercies? Selah.
verses.displayText: Hath God forgotten to be gracious? hath he in anger shut up his tender mercies?
verses.context: Wrestling with doubt, Asaph asks aloud in this psalm whether God has simply stopped being merciful.

verses.text: For a day in thy courts is better than a thousand. I had rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God, than to dwell in the tents of wickedness.
verses.displayText: For a day in thy courts is better than a thousand. I had rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God, than to dwell in the tents of wickedness.
verses.context: Longing simply to be near God's temple, the sons of Korah compare one day there to a thousand anywhere else.

verses.text: For thou, Lord, art good, and ready to forgive; and plenteous in mercy unto all them that call upon thee.
verses.displayText: For thou, Lord, art good, and ready to forgive; and plenteous in mercy unto all them that call upon thee.
verses.context: Calling himself poor and needy in this prayer, David describes God as quick to forgive and full of mercy.

verses.text: Lord, why castest thou off my soul? why hidest thou thy face from me?
verses.displayText: Lord, why castest thou off my soul? why hidest thou thy face from me?
verses.context: One of the darkest psalms, this one written by Heman, a temple musician, asks God directly why he feels abandoned.

verses.text: So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom.
verses.displayText: So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom.
verses.context: Reflecting on how short life is, the writer of this prayer attributed to Moses asks for wisdom about how to spend the time left.

verses.text: He that dwelleth in the secret place of the most High shall abide under the shadow of the Almighty.
verses.displayText: He that dwelleth in the secret place of the most High shall abide under the shadow of the Almighty.
verses.context: With no named author, this psalm opens by describing the safety of a person who stays close to God.

verses.text: I will say of the Lord, He is my refuge and my fortress: my God; in him will I trust.
verses.displayText: I will say of the Lord, He is my refuge and my fortress: my God; in him will I trust.
verses.context: A few lines into the same psalm, the writer responds with his own personal declaration of trust in God.

verses.text: He shall cover thee with his feathers, and under his wings shalt thou trust: his truth shall be thy shield and buckler.
verses.displayText: He shall cover thee with his feathers, and under his wings shalt thou trust: his truth shall be thy shield and buckler.
verses.context: Using the image of a bird's sheltering feathers and wings, the same psalm describes God's protection as something close and constant.

verses.text: For he shall give his angels charge over thee, to keep thee in all thy ways.
verses.displayText: For he shall give his angels charge over thee, to keep thee in all thy ways.
verses.context: This verse from the same psalm is later quoted by the devil while tempting Jesus in the wilderness, according to the Gospels.

verses.text: Let us come before his presence with thanksgiving, and make a joyful noise unto him with psalms.
verses.displayText: Let us come before his presence with thanksgiving, and make a joyful noise unto him with psalms.
verses.context: Part of a call to worship with no named author, this verse invites the reader to come into God's presence giving thanks.

verses.text: Enter into his gates with thanksgiving, and into his courts with praise: be thankful unto him, and bless his name.
verses.displayText: Enter into his gates with thanksgiving, and into his courts with praise: be thankful unto him, and bless his name.
verses.context: Labeled simply a psalm of praise with no named author, this verse instructs worshippers on how to enter the temple courts.

verses.text: Bless the Lord, O my soul, and forget not all his benefits:
verses.displayText: Bless the Lord, O my soul, and forget not all his benefits:
verses.context: David tells his own soul not to forget anything good God has done for him, at the start of this psalm.

verses.text: As far as the east is from the west, so far hath he removed our transgressions from us.
verses.displayText: As far as the east is from the west, so far hath he removed our transgressions from us.
verses.context: A few verses on, David uses the distance between east and west to describe how completely God forgives.

verses.text: O give thanks unto the Lord, for he is good: for his mercy endureth for ever.
verses.displayText: O give thanks unto the Lord, for he is good: for his mercy endureth for ever.
verses.context: Opening a section of thanksgiving psalms with no named author, this verse calls on the reader to give thanks because God is good.

verses.text: What shall I render unto the Lord for all his benefits toward me?
verses.displayText: What shall I render unto the Lord for all his benefits toward me?
verses.context: With no author named, the writer of this psalm asks what he can possibly give back to God for all he has received.

verses.text: Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints.
verses.displayText: Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints.
verses.context: This thanksgiving psalm goes on to say that God values the lives of his faithful people even in their death.

verses.text: This is the day which the Lord hath made; we will rejoice and be glad in it.
verses.displayText: This is the day which the Lord hath made; we will rejoice and be glad in it.
verses.context: Without a named author, this verse from a thanksgiving psalm celebrates the present day as something God himself made.

verses.text: נ NUN. Thy word is a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my path.
verses.displayText: Thy word is a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my path.
verses.context: From the Bible's longest chapter, an alphabetic psalm with no named author, this verse compares God's word to a lamp for walking at night.

verses.text: A Song of degrees. I will lift up mine eyes unto the hills, from whence cometh my help.
verses.displayText: I will lift up mine eyes unto the hills, from whence cometh my help.
verses.context: Part of a set of psalms called 'songs of ascents,' likely sung by travelers heading up to Jerusalem, this one asks where help truly comes from.

verses.text: They that sow in tears shall reap in joy.
verses.displayText: They that sow in tears shall reap in joy.
verses.context: This 'song of ascents' compares hard work done through tears to a harvest that eventually comes in with joy.

verses.text: A Song of degrees of David. Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity!
verses.displayText: Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity!
verses.context: David wrote this 'song of ascents,' celebrating the simple pleasure of family or community getting along peacefully.

verses.text: Whither shall I go from thy spirit? or whither shall I flee from thy presence?
verses.displayText: Whither shall I go from thy spirit? or whither shall I flee from thy presence?
verses.context: In a psalm about being fully known by God, David asks whether there's anywhere at all he could go to escape that presence.

verses.text: I will praise thee; for I am fearfully and wonderfully made: marvellous are thy works; and that my soul knoweth right well.
verses.displayText: I will praise thee; for I am fearfully and wonderfully made: marvellous are thy works; and that my soul knoweth right well.
verses.context: Continuing to reflect on how closely he was made and known, David praises God himself for crafting him so carefully.

verses.text: Search me, O God, and know my heart: try me, and know my thoughts:
verses.displayText: Search me, O God, and know my heart: try me, and know my thoughts:
verses.context: Near the end of the same psalm, after admitting he hates his enemies, David asks God to search his own heart instead.

verses.text: He healeth the broken in heart, and bindeth up their wounds.
verses.displayText: He healeth the broken in heart, and bindeth up their wounds.
verses.context: In a hymn praising God for rebuilding Jerusalem, this verse describes God's care for people who are grieving.

verses.text: Let every thing that hath breath praise the Lord. Praise ye the Lord.
verses.displayText: Let every thing that hath breath praise the Lord. Praise ye the Lord.
verses.context: This final verse of the entire book of Psalms calls on every living, breathing thing to join in praise.

verses.text: The fear of the Lord is the beginning of knowledge: but fools despise wisdom and instruction.
verses.displayText: The fear of the Lord is the beginning of knowledge: but fools despise wisdom and instruction.
verses.context: Near the start of the book, this proverb sets up fearing God as the starting point for actually knowing anything worthwhile.

verses.text: Trust in the Lord with all thine heart; and lean not unto thine own understanding.
verses.displayText: Trust in the Lord with all thine heart; and lean not unto thine own understanding.
verses.context: Solomon, addressing this collection of sayings to 'my son,' tells him to trust God rather than lean only on his own reasoning.

verses.text: In all thy ways acknowledge him, and he shall direct thy paths.
verses.displayText: In all thy ways acknowledge him, and he shall direct thy paths.
verses.context: The next line in the same proverb tells the reader that including God in every decision will keep their path straight.

verses.text: Keep thy heart with all diligence; for out of it are the issues of life.
verses.displayText: Keep thy heart with all diligence; for out of it are the issues of life.
verses.context: In a father's advice to his son, this proverb singles out the heart as the thing most worth guarding closely.

verses.text: Hatred stirreth up strifes: but love covereth all sins.
verses.displayText: Hatred stirreth up strifes: but love covereth all sins.
verses.context: One of Solomon's short, paired sayings, this proverb contrasts what hatred stirs up with what love is able to cover.

verses.text: Heaviness in the heart of man maketh it stoop: but a good word maketh it glad.
verses.displayText: Heaviness in the heart of man maketh it stoop: but a good word maketh it glad.
verses.context: In this short proverb, Solomon notes how a heavy heart weighs a person down, but a kind word can lift it.

verses.text: Hope deferred maketh the heart sick: but when the desire cometh, it is a tree of life.
verses.displayText: Hope deferred maketh the heart sick: but when the desire cometh, it is a tree of life.
verses.context: Among Solomon's proverbs about everyday life, this one names the ache of a delayed hope and the relief when what's wanted finally comes.

verses.text: There is a way which seemeth right unto a man, but the end thereof are the ways of death.
verses.displayText: There is a way which seemeth right unto a man, but the end thereof are the ways of death.
verses.context: Solomon warns his readers in this collection of sayings that a path can feel completely right to a person and still end in death.

verses.text: A soft answer turneth away wrath: but grievous words stir up anger.
verses.displayText: A soft answer turneth away wrath: but grievous words stir up anger.
verses.context: One of Solomon's proverbs about speech, this one contrasts a gentle reply with words that provoke anger.

verses.text: Commit thy works unto the Lord, and thy thoughts shall be established.
verses.displayText: Commit thy works unto the Lord, and thy thoughts shall be established.
verses.context: Speaking as a father instructing his son, Solomon advises handing your plans over to God as the way to see them succeed.

verses.text: A man’s heart deviseth his way: but the Lord directeth his steps.
verses.displayText: A man’s heart deviseth his way: but the Lord directeth his steps.
verses.context: In this collection of practical sayings, Solomon admits people plan their own course, but credits God with directing where their steps land.

verses.text: Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall.
verses.displayText: Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall.
verses.context: One of Solomon's short warnings to his son, this saying cautions that overconfidence tends to come right before a fall.

verses.text: A friend loveth at all times, and a brother is born for adversity.
verses.displayText: A friend loveth at all times, and a brother is born for adversity.
verses.context: Solomon, teaching his son about relationships, distinguishes a friend's constant loyalty from a brother's loyalty specifically in hard times.

verses.text: A merry heart doeth good like a medicine: but a broken spirit drieth the bones.
verses.displayText: A merry heart doeth good like a medicine: but a broken spirit drieth the bones.
verses.context: Among his sayings about daily life, Solomon compares a cheerful outlook to medicine, and a crushed spirit to something that wears the body down.

verses.text: The name of the Lord is a strong tower: the righteous runneth into it, and is safe.
verses.displayText: The name of the Lord is a strong tower: the righteous runneth into it, and is safe.
verses.context: Teaching his son to trust God for safety, Solomon here pictures God's name as a fortified tower the righteous can run into.

verses.text: A man that hath friends must shew himself friendly: and there is a friend that sticketh closer than a brother.
verses.displayText: A man that hath friends must shew himself friendly: and there is a friend that sticketh closer than a brother.
verses.context: Solomon tells his son to be the kind of friend worth having, then points to a friend who sticks closer than a brother would.

verses.text: There are many devices in a man’s heart; nevertheless the counsel of the Lord, that shall stand.
verses.displayText: There are many devices in a man’s heart; nevertheless the counsel of the Lord, that shall stand.
verses.context: In this collection of Solomon's sayings, many plans fill a person's mind, but only God's own plan is said to hold up.

verses.text: Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it.
verses.displayText: Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it.
verses.context: This proverb offers a father's confidence that early training in a child's life will shape the direction of their adult life.

verses.text: For a just man falleth seven times, and riseth up again: but the wicked shall fall into mischief.
verses.displayText: For a just man falleth seven times, and riseth up again: but the wicked shall fall into mischief.
verses.context: Solomon assures his son here that even a good person stumbles again and again, yet keeps getting back up each time.

verses.text: Iron sharpeneth iron; so a man sharpeneth the countenance of his friend.
verses.displayText: Iron sharpeneth iron; so a man sharpeneth the countenance of his friend.
verses.context: Teaching his son about friendship, Solomon pictures two pieces of iron sharpening each other as what one friend can do for another.

verses.text: He that covereth his sins shall not prosper: but whoso confesseth and forsaketh them shall have mercy.
verses.displayText: He that covereth his sins shall not prosper: but whoso confesseth and forsaketh them shall have mercy.
verses.context: Among sayings about honesty, Solomon contrasts hiding wrongdoing, which never works, with admitting it, which leads to mercy.

verses.text: Where there is no vision, the people perish: but he that keepeth the law, happy is he.
verses.displayText: Where there is no vision, the people perish: but he that keepeth the law, happy is he.
verses.context: Solomon warns his son in this saying that people lose their way when they have no larger vision guiding them.

verses.text: Favour is deceitful, and beauty is vain: but a woman that feareth the Lord, she shall be praised.
verses.displayText: Favour is deceitful, and beauty is vain: but a woman that feareth the Lord, she shall be praised.
verses.context: Near the close of a poem, part of what King Lemuel's mother taught him about a capable woman, this line says fearing God outlasts charm and beauty.

verses.text: Vanity of vanities, saith the Preacher, vanity of vanities; all is vanity.
verses.displayText: Vanity of vanities, saith the Preacher, vanity of vanities; all is vanity.
verses.context: Writing as 'the Preacher,' a king in Jerusalem reflecting on his life, this opens the book by declaring everything he chased amounts to nothing lasting.

verses.text: To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven:
verses.displayText: To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven:
verses.context: Writing as 'the Preacher' reflecting on the shape of life, the writer opens this list by saying every activity has its own proper time.

verses.text: He hath made every thing beautiful in his time: also he hath set the world in their heart, so that no man can find out the work that God maketh from the beginning to the end.
verses.displayText: He hath made every thing beautiful in his time: also he hath set the world in their heart, so that no man can find out the work that God maketh from the beginning to the end.
verses.context: Continuing the same reflection on times and seasons, the Preacher says people sense something lasting beyond what they can fully grasp.

verses.text: Two are better than one; because they have a good reward for their labour.
verses.displayText: Two are better than one; because they have a good reward for their labour.
verses.context: In the middle of reflecting on the emptiness of working alone, the Preacher points out that two people working together do better than one.

verses.text: Whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do it with thy might; for there is no work, nor device, nor knowledge, nor wisdom, in the grave, whither thou goest.
verses.displayText: Whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do it with thy might; for there is no work, nor device, nor knowledge, nor wisdom, in the grave, whither thou goest.
verses.context: The Preacher, reflecting on how short life is, urges the reader to throw full effort into whatever they're doing while they're still alive.

verses.text: Let us hear the conclusion of the whole matter: Fear God, and keep his commandments: for this is the whole duty of man.
verses.displayText: Let us hear the conclusion of the whole matter: Fear God, and keep his commandments: for this is the whole duty of man.
verses.context: This closes the entire book, with the Preacher summing up everything he has said in one final piece of advice.

verses.text: I am my beloved’s, and my beloved is mine: he feedeth among the lilies.
verses.displayText: I am my beloved’s, and my beloved is mine: he feedeth among the lilies.
verses.context: In this love poem attributed to Solomon, the woman speaking affirms her mutual belonging with the man she loves.

verses.text: Many waters cannot quench love, neither can the floods drown it: if a man would give all the substance of his house for love, it would utterly be contemned.
verses.displayText: Many waters cannot quench love, neither can the floods drown it: if a man would give all the substance of his house for love, it would utterly be contemned.
verses.context: Near the end of the same love poem, the woman describes love as something no flood or fortune could buy or destroy.

verses.text: Come now, and let us reason together, saith the Lord: though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow; though they be red like crimson, they shall be as wool.
verses.displayText: Come now, and let us reason together, saith the Lord: though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow; though they be red like crimson, they shall be as wool.
verses.context: Confronting a nation that had kept up religious rituals while ignoring justice, God invites them through Isaiah to reason honestly with him.

verses.text: And he shall judge among the nations, and shall rebuke many people: and they shall beat their swords into plowshares, and their spears into pruninghooks: nation shall not lift up sword against nation, neither shall they learn war any more.
verses.displayText: And he shall judge among the nations, and shall rebuke many people: and they shall beat their swords into plowshares, and their spears into pruninghooks: nation shall not lift up sword against nation, neither shall they learn war any more.
verses.context: In a vision about the future given to the prophet Isaiah, weapons of war are described being turned into farming tools.

verses.text: Also I heard the voice of the Lord, saying, Whom shall I send, and who will go for us? Then said I, Here am I; send me.
verses.displayText: Also I heard the voice of the Lord, saying, Whom shall I send, and who will go for us? Then said I, Here am I; send me.
verses.context: After seeing a vision of God in the temple and having his own guilt dealt with, Isaiah hears God asking for someone to send, and volunteers.

verses.text: Therefore the Lord himself shall give you a sign; Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel.
verses.displayText: Therefore the Lord himself shall give you a sign; Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel.
verses.context: Speaking to a frightened king named Ahaz, Isaiah gives a sign involving a coming child; Matthew's Gospel later applies this to the birth of Jesus.

verses.text: For unto us a child is born, unto us a son is given: and the government shall be upon his shoulder: and his name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, The mighty God, The everlasting Father, The Prince of Peace.
verses.displayText: For unto us a child is born, unto us a son is given: and the government shall be upon his shoulder: and his name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, The mighty God, The everlasting Father, The Prince of Peace.
verses.context: In a passage about a future ruler bringing lasting peace, Isaiah names several titles this coming child will carry.

verses.text: The wolf also shall dwell with the lamb, and the leopard shall lie down with the kid; and the calf and the young lion and the fatling together; and a little child shall lead them.
verses.displayText: The wolf also shall dwell with the lamb, and the leopard shall lie down with the kid; and the calf and the young lion and the fatling together; and a little child shall lead them.
verses.context: Describing a future age of peace under a coming ruler, Isaiah pictures natural enemies among animals living safely side by side.

verses.text: Behold, God is my salvation; I will trust, and not be afraid: for the Lord Jehovah is my strength and my song; he also is become my salvation.
verses.displayText: Behold, God is my salvation; I will trust, and not be afraid: for the Lord Jehovah is my strength and my song; he also is become my salvation.
verses.context: This is a short song of thanks Isaiah gives the people to sing about a coming day when God's anger has passed.

verses.text: Thou wilt keep him in perfect peace, whose mind is stayed on thee: because he trusteth in thee.
verses.displayText: Thou wilt keep him in perfect peace, whose mind is stayed on thee: because he trusteth in thee.
verses.context: Part of a song Isaiah gives Judah to sing, this verse describes steady peace for anyone whose mind stays fixed on God.

verses.text: And thine ears shall hear a word behind thee, saying, This is the way, walk ye in it, when ye turn to the right hand, and when ye turn to the left.
verses.displayText: And thine ears shall hear a word behind thee, saying, This is the way, walk ye in it, when ye turn to the right hand, and when ye turn to the left.
verses.context: Speaking of a future time when the people finally listen to their teachers, Isaiah describes a voice guiding them which way to turn.

verses.text: The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever.
verses.displayText: The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever.
verses.context: Opening a new section of comfort for a discouraged nation, Isaiah contrasts how quickly people fade with how permanent God's word is.

verses.text: He shall feed his flock like a shepherd: he shall gather the lambs with his arm, and carry them in his bosom, and shall gently lead those that are with young.
verses.displayText: He shall feed his flock like a shepherd: he shall gather the lambs with his arm, and carry them in his bosom, and shall gently lead those that are with young.
verses.context: In the same passage of comfort, Isaiah pictures God tending his people gently, the way a shepherd carries young lambs.

verses.text: He giveth power to the faint; and to them that have no might he increaseth strength.
verses.displayText: He giveth power to the faint; and to them that have no might he increaseth strength.
verses.context: Speaking to an exhausted, discouraged nation, Isaiah describes a God who gives strength to people who have none left.

verses.text: But they that wait upon the Lord shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles; they shall run, and not be weary; and they shall walk, and not faint.
verses.displayText: But they that wait upon the Lord shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles; they shall run, and not be weary; and they shall walk, and not faint.
verses.context: This closes the same passage, promising that people who keep waiting on God will find their strength renewed.

verses.text: Fear thou not; for I am with thee: be not dismayed; for I am thy God: I will strengthen thee; yea, I will help thee; yea, I will uphold thee with the right hand of my righteousness.
verses.displayText: Fear thou not; for I am with thee: be not dismayed; for I am thy God: I will strengthen thee; yea, I will help thee; yea, I will uphold thee with the right hand of my righteousness.
verses.context: Speaking to a fearful, exiled people, Isaiah delivers this reassurance from God not to be afraid, because God will hold them up.

verses.text: But now thus saith the Lord that created thee, O Jacob, and he that formed thee, O Israel, Fear not: for I have redeemed thee, I have called thee by thy name; thou art mine.
verses.displayText: But now thus saith the Lord that created thee, O Jacob, and he that formed thee, O Israel, Fear not: for I have redeemed thee, I have called thee by thy name; thou art mine.
verses.context: Speaking to a people who felt abandoned, Isaiah delivers God's message that they still belong to him by name.

verses.text: When thou passest through the waters, I will be with thee; and through the rivers, they shall not overflow thee: when thou walkest through the fire, thou shalt not be burned; neither shall the flame kindle upon thee.
verses.displayText: When thou passest through the waters, I will be with thee; and through the rivers, they shall not overflow thee: when thou walkest through the fire, thou shalt not be burned; neither shall the flame kindle upon thee.
verses.context: Continuing the same message, Isaiah describes God's presence with the people through danger, using water and fire as pictures.

verses.text: Behold, I will do a new thing; now it shall spring forth; shall ye not know it? I will even make a way in the wilderness, and rivers in the desert.
verses.displayText: Behold, I will do a new thing; now it shall spring forth; shall ye not know it? I will even make a way in the wilderness, and rivers in the desert.
verses.context: In a message about restoration after hardship, Isaiah has God announce something new, like a road appearing through empty desert.

verses.text: I, even I, am he that blotteth out thy transgressions for mine own sake, and will not remember thy sins.
verses.displayText: I, even I, am he that blotteth out thy transgressions for mine own sake, and will not remember thy sins.
verses.context: Speaking for God to a people who had grown distant, Isaiah delivers a promise that their wrongs will be forgotten, not held against them.

verses.text: Can a woman forget her sucking child, that she should not have compassion on the son of her womb? yea, they may forget, yet will I not forget thee.
verses.displayText: Can a woman forget her sucking child, that she should not have compassion on the son of her womb? yea, they may forget, yet will I not forget thee.
verses.context: Isaiah compares God's care to something even stronger than a mother's bond with her nursing child.

verses.text: Behold, I have graven thee upon the palms of my hands; thy walls are continually before me.
verses.displayText: Behold, I have graven thee upon the palms of my hands; thy walls are continually before me.
verses.context: Right after comparing God to a mother, Isaiah pictures the people themselves engraved permanently on the palms of God's own hands.

verses.text: He is despised and rejected of men; a man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief: and we hid as it were our faces from him; he was despised, and we esteemed him not.
verses.displayText: He is despised and rejected of men; a man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief: and we hid as it were our faces from him; he was despised, and we esteemed him not.
verses.context: Describing a suffering servant figure rejected by those around him, Isaiah writes lines the New Testament later applies to Jesus.

verses.text: Surely he hath borne our griefs, and carried our sorrows: yet we did esteem him stricken, smitten of God, and afflicted.
verses.displayText: Surely he hath borne our griefs, and carried our sorrows: yet we did esteem him stricken, smitten of God, and afflicted.
verses.context: Continuing the same description, Isaiah pictures this servant carrying suffering that wasn't originally his own.

verses.text: But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed.
verses.displayText: But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed.
verses.context: Still describing the suffering servant, Isaiah connects this figure's wounds to healing for others, a passage Peter later quotes about Jesus.

verses.text: All we like sheep have gone astray; we have turned every one to his own way; and the Lord hath laid on him the iniquity of us all.
verses.displayText: All we like sheep have gone astray; we have turned every one to his own way; and the Lord hath laid on him the iniquity of us all.
verses.context: This verse pictures people wandering like lost sheep, with their wrongdoing placed instead onto the suffering servant Isaiah describes.

verses.text: No weapon that is formed against thee shall prosper; and every tongue that shall rise against thee in judgment thou shalt condemn. This is the heritage of the servants of the Lord, and their righteousness is of me, saith the Lord.
verses.displayText: No weapon that is formed against thee shall prosper; and every tongue that shall rise against thee in judgment thou shalt condemn. This is the heritage of the servants of the Lord, and their righteousness is of me, saith the Lord.
verses.context: In a passage of comfort after judgment, Isaiah promises that no weapon aimed at God's people will ultimately succeed.

verses.text: For my thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways my ways, saith the Lord.
verses.displayText: For my thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways my ways, saith the Lord.
verses.context: Inviting people to turn back to God, Isaiah has God explain that his thinking works differently than human thinking does.

verses.text: Arise, shine; for thy light is come, and the glory of the Lord is risen upon thee.
verses.displayText: Arise, shine; for thy light is come, and the glory of the Lord is risen upon thee.
verses.context: Opening a vision of future restoration for Jerusalem, Isaiah calls the city to rise because light has arrived.

verses.text: But now, O Lord, thou art our father; we are the clay, and thou our potter; and we all are the work of thy hand.
verses.displayText: But now, O Lord, thou art our father; we are the clay, and thou our potter; and we all are the work of thy hand.
verses.context: Praying on behalf of a guilty nation, Isaiah pictures God as a potter shaping his people like clay.

verses.text: As one whom his mother comforteth, so will I comfort you; and ye shall be comforted in Jerusalem.
verses.displayText: As one whom his mother comforteth, so will I comfort you; and ye shall be comforted in Jerusalem.
verses.context: Near the end of the book, Isaiah promises Jerusalem comfort like that of a mother comforting her child.

verses.text: Before I formed thee in the belly I knew thee; and before thou camest forth out of the womb I sanctified thee, and I ordained thee a prophet unto the nations.
verses.displayText: Before I formed thee in the belly I knew thee; and before thou camest forth out of the womb I sanctified thee, and I ordained thee a prophet unto the nations.
verses.context: At the start of his call to be a prophet, Jeremiah hears God say he was known and appointed before he was even born.

verses.text: Blessed is the man that trusteth in the Lord, and whose hope the Lord is.
verses.displayText: Blessed is the man that trusteth in the Lord, and whose hope the Lord is.
verses.context: In a passage contrasting two kinds of people, Jeremiah describes the one who trusts in God as genuinely fortunate.

verses.text: The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked: who can know it?
verses.displayText: The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked: who can know it?
verses.context: Right after describing the trusting person, Jeremiah adds this blunt warning about how easily the human heart deceives itself.

verses.text: For I know the thoughts that I think toward you, saith the Lord, thoughts of peace, and not of evil, to give you an expected end.
verses.displayText: For I know the thoughts that I think toward you, saith the Lord, thoughts of peace, and not of evil, to give you an expected end.
verses.context: Writing a letter to exiles settled in Babylon, Jeremiah passes along God's message that their future still holds hope.

verses.text: And ye shall seek me, and find me, when ye shall search for me with all your heart.
verses.displayText: And ye shall seek me, and find me, when ye shall search for me with all your heart.
verses.context: Continuing the same letter to the exiles, Jeremiah says that searching for God wholeheartedly is how they'll find him.

verses.text: The Lord hath appeared of old unto me, saying, Yea, I have loved thee with an everlasting love: therefore with lovingkindness have I drawn thee.
verses.displayText: The Lord hath appeared of old unto me, saying, Yea, I have loved thee with an everlasting love: therefore with lovingkindness have I drawn thee.
verses.context: In a message of restoration to exiled Israel, Jeremiah describes God's love for the nation as lasting and unbroken.

verses.text: Call unto me, and I will answer thee, and shew thee great and mighty things, which thou knowest not.
verses.displayText: Call unto me, and I will answer thee, and shew thee great and mighty things, which thou knowest not.
verses.context: Speaking to Jeremiah while he was imprisoned during the siege of Jerusalem, God invites him to call out and expect an answer.

verses.text: It is of the Lord’s mercies that we are not consumed, because his compassions fail not.
verses.displayText: It is of the Lord’s mercies that we are not consumed, because his compassions fail not.
verses.context: Mourning the destruction of Jerusalem, the writer of Lamentations pauses to say that God's mercy is the reason anything remains.

verses.text: They are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness.
verses.displayText: They are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness.
verses.context: Right after that admission, the same writer describes God's faithfulness as something renewed every single morning.

verses.text: It is good that a man should both hope and quietly wait for the salvation of the Lord.
verses.displayText: It is good that a man should both hope and quietly wait for the salvation of the Lord.
verses.context: Still grieving the city's fall, the writer of Lamentations concludes that waiting quietly for God's rescue is the better path.

verses.text: A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you: and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you an heart of flesh.
verses.displayText: A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you: and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you an heart of flesh.
verses.context: Speaking to exiles in Babylon, Ezekiel delivers God's promise of an inner change, replacing a hardened heart with a responsive one.

verses.text: Thus saith the Lord God unto these bones; Behold, I will cause breath to enter into you, and ye shall live:
verses.displayText: Thus saith the Lord God unto these bones; Behold, I will cause breath to enter into you, and ye shall live:
verses.context: In a vision of a valley full of dry bones, Ezekiel hears God promise to breathe life back into them.

verses.text: And said, O man greatly beloved, fear not: peace be unto thee, be strong, yea, be strong. And when he had spoken unto me, I was strengthened, and said, Let my lord speak; for thou hast strengthened me.
verses.displayText: And said, O man greatly beloved, fear not: peace be unto thee, be strong, yea, be strong. And when he had spoken unto me, I was strengthened, and said, Let my lord speak; for thou hast strengthened me.
verses.context: After a terrifying vision leaves Daniel weak and speechless, a heavenly messenger tells him not to be afraid and strengthens him.

verses.text: For I desired mercy, and not sacrifice; and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings.
verses.displayText: For I desired mercy, and not sacrifice; and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings.
verses.context: Speaking to a nation going through the motions of worship, Hosea delivers God's preference for genuine care over empty ritual; Jesus later quotes this line.

verses.text: I will heal their backsliding, I will love them freely: for mine anger is turned away from him.
verses.displayText: I will heal their backsliding, I will love them freely: for mine anger is turned away from him.
verses.context: Closing his book with a call to return to God, Hosea delivers a promise that God will heal Israel's wandering and love them freely.

verses.text: And I will restore to you the years that the locust hath eaten, the cankerworm, and the caterpiller, and the palmerworm, my great army which I sent among you.
verses.displayText: And I will restore to you the years that the locust hath eaten, the cankerworm, and the caterpiller, and the palmerworm, my great army which I sent among you.
verses.context: After a locust plague had stripped the land bare, Joel delivers God's promise to restore what those years had eaten away.

verses.text: But let judgment run down as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream.
verses.displayText: But let judgment run down as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream.
verses.context: Rejecting a nation's religious festivals while injustice continued, Amos calls instead for fairness to flow like a constant stream.

verses.text: And said, I cried by reason of mine affliction unto the Lord, and he heard me; out of the belly of hell cried I, and thou heardest my voice.
verses.displayText: And said, I cried by reason of mine affliction unto the Lord, and he heard me; out of the belly of hell cried I, and thou heardest my voice.
verses.context: Swallowed by a great fish after running from God, Jonah prays this line from inside its belly.

verses.text: He hath shewed thee, O man, what is good; and what doth the Lord require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?
verses.displayText: He hath shewed thee, O man, what is good; and what doth the Lord require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?
verses.context: Answering the question of what sacrifice could possibly please God, Micah says God has already made it simple.

verses.text: He will turn again, he will have compassion upon us; he will subdue our iniquities; and thou wilt cast all their sins into the depths of the sea.
verses.displayText: He will turn again, he will have compassion upon us; he will subdue our iniquities; and thou wilt cast all their sins into the depths of the sea.
verses.context: Closing his book with hope after chapters of warning, Micah pictures God throwing the nation's sins into the depths of the sea.

verses.text: The Lord is good, a strong hold in the day of trouble; and he knoweth them that trust in him.
verses.displayText: The Lord is good, a strong hold in the day of trouble; and he knoweth them that trust in him.
verses.context: In a book largely about coming judgment on Nineveh, Nahum pauses to describe God as a safe place for anyone who trusts him.

verses.text: O Lord, how long shall I cry, and thou wilt not hear! even cry out unto thee of violence, and thou wilt not save!
verses.displayText: O Lord, how long shall I cry, and thou wilt not hear! even cry out unto thee of violence, and thou wilt not save!
verses.context: Opening his book with a complaint, the prophet Habakkuk asks God how long he must cry out about violence before being heard.

verses.text: The Lord God is my strength, and he will make my feet like hinds’ feet, and he will make me to walk upon mine high places. To the chief singer on my stringed instruments.
verses.displayText: The Lord God is my strength, and he will make my feet like hinds’ feet, and he will make me to walk upon mine high places.
verses.context: Closing his book after wrestling with God over injustice, Habakkuk declares his strength in God even if the harvest completely fails.

verses.text: The Lord thy God in the midst of thee is mighty; he will save, he will rejoice over thee with joy; he will rest in his love, he will joy over thee with singing.
verses.displayText: The Lord thy God in the midst of thee is mighty; he will save, he will rejoice over thee with joy; he will rest in his love, he will joy over thee with singing.
verses.context: In a passage promising restoration for Jerusalem, Zephaniah describes God not just saving his people but delighting in them with singing.

verses.text: Then he answered and spake unto me, saying, This is the word of the Lord unto Zerubbabel, saying, Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the Lord of hosts.
verses.displayText: Then he answered and spake unto me, saying, This is the word of the Lord unto Zerubbabel, saying, Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the Lord of hosts.
verses.context: Giving Zerubbabel encouragement for rebuilding the temple, an angel delivers this message that the work depends on God's spirit, not on force.

verses.text: But he answered and said, It is written, Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of God.
verses.displayText: But he answered and said, It is written, Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of God.
verses.context: Fasting alone in the wilderness, Jesus responds to the devil's suggestion that he turn stones into bread by quoting Deuteronomy.

verses.text: Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.
verses.displayText: Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.
verses.context: This opens the Sermon on the Mount, where Jesus sits down before a crowd on a hillside and begins teaching his disciples.

verses.text: Blessed are they that mourn: for they shall be comforted.
verses.displayText: Blessed are they that mourn: for they shall be comforted.
verses.context: Continuing that same hillside teaching, Jesus names people who are grieving as among those who will be comforted.

verses.text: Blessed are the meek: for they shall inherit the earth.
verses.displayText: Blessed are the meek: for they shall inherit the earth.
verses.context: Still in the same teaching, Jesus says people who don't push their way to the front will end up inheriting the earth.

verses.text: Blessed are they which do hunger and thirst after righteousness: for they shall be filled.
verses.displayText: Blessed are they which do hunger and thirst after righteousness: for they shall be filled.
verses.context: Continuing the same list, Jesus describes people who are hungry for things to be made right as people who will be satisfied.

verses.text: Blessed are the merciful: for they shall obtain mercy.
verses.displayText: Blessed are the merciful: for they shall obtain mercy.
verses.context: Further into the same teaching, Jesus connects showing mercy to others with receiving mercy in return.

verses.text: Blessed are the pure in heart: for they shall see God.
verses.displayText: Blessed are the pure in heart: for they shall see God.
verses.context: Still teaching the crowd on the hillside, Jesus says people with undivided, honest hearts are the ones who will see God.

verses.text: Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God.
verses.displayText: Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God.
verses.context: In this same hillside teaching known as the Beatitudes, Jesus calls people who make peace the ones who will be recognized as God's children.

verses.text: Ye are the light of the world. A city that is set on an hill cannot be hid.
verses.displayText: Ye are the light of the world. A city that is set on an hill cannot be hid.
verses.context: Continuing the same hillside teaching, Jesus tells his listeners they are the light of the world, like a city set on a hill that cannot be hidden.

verses.text: Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven.
